name: Consistency and Standards
description: Users should not have to relearn the same thing on each screen; repeated patterns, terminology, and platform conventions should mean the same thing each time.
design_relevance_note: Central to component libraries, cross-platform parity decisions, labeling systems, interaction patterns, iconography, and choosing when not to reinvent native conventions.
myth_risk_note: No on-topic peer-reviewed evidence was discovered to support the heuristic. Existing corpus context confirms nearby but distinct material exists (Jakob's Law on convention-following) but no direct validation of Nielsen's full consistency-and-standards heuristic. Consistent with this entry's existing no_rigorous_backing_found status.
prevalence_note: Nielsen heuristic #4, deeply embedded in design-system work and standard UX critique whenever teams debate whether to follow or break a convention.

applications.title: Jakob Nielsen: 1980s market research found Macintosh's UI consistency drove more software sales than DOS
applications.description: In his own 2002 preface to a reprint of 'Coordinating User Interfaces for Consistency,' Jakob Nielsen recalls that 1980s market research found Macintosh users bought more software packages than DOS users, specifically because Apple's emphasis on interface consistency made it easier for users to learn each additional package -- a real, quantifiable business advantage from consistency that Nielsen estimated was 'worth millions of dollars' at 1980s software-market scale.
applications.ethical_note: A genuine efficiency/usability benefit for users (easier learning transfer between applications) that also produced a real commercial advantage for the platform -- no persuasion-vs-user-interest tension, a case where consistency served both sides at once. Nielsen's own follow-up point (written in 2002, now itself a historical artifact) is worth preserving too: he argued the economic stakes of consistency had grown from 'millions' in the 1980s software market to 'hundreds of billions' in wasted intranet-era employee productivity -- a claim about scale, not independently verified, but illustrative of how the same principle's stated economic stakes can be reported very differently across sources and eras.

applications.title: Sutter Health's shifting 'Finish Later' button position in appointment check-in
applications.description: In Sutter Health's multipage online appointment check-in form (collecting payment, allergy, and health information), the 'Finish Later' button sits to the right of the primary submit button on the first two screens, then swaps to the left on a later screen -- an internal-consistency violation that led users to accidentally tap 'Finish Later' instead of submitting, only discovering afterward they were never checked in.
applications.ethical_note: This is a structural usability error, not a persuasion technique -- there is no evidence Sutter Health intended the inconsistent button placement to mislead patients, and the harm (patients believing they completed check-in when they hadn't) is a byproduct of design carelessness rather than a deliberate dark pattern. Graded not_applicable because there is no persuasion or manipulation dimension to weigh here, unlike anchoring or scarcity applications elsewhere in this corpus.
